title: 4. Pillars, Tone, Themes, and Narrative Goals Established
use_cases: Use when establishing the foundational tenets of a game's story and mechanics
Implement when bridging original IP themes with new game development
Configure when defining the emotional atmosphere and mood for cross-disciplinary teams
Use when aligning narrative goals with art, music, and design systems
Configure when determining the centrality and role of storytelling in the project scope
content:
#### NARRATIVE PILLARS

Pillars are foundational principles that inform the game’s mechanics, systems, and core experience. They are tenets that drive the development process.

![Narrative Blog Part 2.png](https://blindsquirrel-staging-media.sfo3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/191653c561c5ade671f08f1cf49398c6.png)

Design usually has its own set of pillars for the game’s mechanics. Narrative pillars inform how the narrative is conceptualized and integrated. I like to ensure the narrative pillars complement or enhance the design pillars.

For Cosmorons, the narrative pillars are:

Expendability and morbid humor

- Irreverent humor, often stemming from the Drudge's expendable nature (which they embrace just as much as the Overlords do), underlies the world’s comedic scenarios.

Satire

- The game subtly pokes fun at the futility of empire, the unquenchable thirst for power and expansion, corporate greed, indoctrination, and war.

Infinite loop

- The core gameplay loop mirrors a humorous looping narrative in which the characters are on a never-ending quest to reach the end of the universe.

When working with other companies’ IP, the first thing I do is read, watch, and analyze anything I can get my hands on to identify the core pillars (I am one of the rare few who use their literature degree daily). They are the most important aspect of anchoring our game in that world.

#### THEMES

Themes are central, recurring ideas that underlie the entire game. Themes differ from pillars in that they’re more emotional and/or philosophical. If the pillars are the bones, the theme is the soul.

![1.png](https://blindsquirrel-staging-media.sfo3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/779f18c0268dddc57f5a642e44604570.png)

Usually, themes don’t emerge until you start developing the story in earnest, but if I’m working with someone else’s IP, whether that’s a film, book, or game series, identifying the themes early on helps unify my ideas with the original IP. Unlike the pillars, they don’t have to be the same themes as the original, but using variations of an IP’s themes plants us more firmly in their world.

Some works have one theme, some have several. It’s important not to have too many, or the emotional core of the story will be muddy. Having too much to say results in not saying much at all.

Examples of themes: blood is thicker than water; corruption of justice; love conquers all; self-acceptance; the inevitable decay of empire.

#### TONE

![2.png](https://blindsquirrel-staging-media.sfo3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/37dd4cc863cd9427983289f656f6287b.png)

Tone is the emotional atmosphere or mood of the game. It informs every aspect of game development, from narrative to art to music to design.

Tone helps ensure everyone is working in the same mindset and all is cohesive.

For narrative, tone impacts story type, its outcomes, the style of humor (if any), dialogue style, and character arcs.

Examples: Whimsical kids' cartoon. Melancholic wonder. Magical realm with creeping darkness. Zany, stylized sci-fi. Cozy, nostalgic fantasy.

#### NARRATIVE GOALS

Narrative’s role is different in every game. Sometimes it’s the core feature; sometimes it’s barely suggested. At the start of planning, I ask the following:

- What is the narrative’s role in this game?
- How central is it?
- What is its importance to the game and its role in selling the experience?

How you answer these will inform your narrative scope and execution.
